title: Why a command is not found
objectives: Explain the PATH as the ordered list of folders the shell searches
Predict which program runs when two folders hold the same name
Fix a command that is not found, including in a window opened before an install

screens.prose: Ana types `ls`. Before anything runs, her shell must find a program called `ls`. It opens folders in the order of the arrows, and runs the first `ls` it finds.
screens.question: Tap every folder the shell opens while it hunts for `ls`.

hints.text: Does the shell know in advance which folder holds `ls`?
It always starts at folder 1.
Folders 1 and 2 hold no `ls`, so it moves on each time, and finds `ls` in folder 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrows from folder 1 until a folder holds `ls`.

byKey.jumped: You went straight to the folder holding `ls`. The shell cannot know where it is: it must look in 1 and 2 first.
byKey.two: You stopped before finding it. Neither 1 nor 2 holds `ls`, so the shell opens folder 3 too.

explain.text: You followed the arrows: no `ls` in folder 1 or 2, so on to folder 3. The shell does this hunt for every command you type. It takes microseconds.

screens.prose: Now Ana types `python3`. This time two folders hold a program with that name: the Python she installed, and the one her Mac came with.
screens.question: Tap the program the shell runs.

hints.text: Which folder does the shell open first?
Folder 1 already holds a `python3`.

feedback.correct: The shell stops at folder 1 and runs Python 3.12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The shell runs the first match it meets.

byKey.ub-py: You picked the Mac's own Python in folder 2. The shell never reaches it: it stops at the first match, in folder 1.

explain.text: You picked the `python3` in folder 1. The shell stopped there and never looked further. The copy in folder 2 is still on the disk, hidden behind the first.

screens.prose:
The ordered list of folders the shell searches is the **PATH**. Ana can print hers; the colons separate the folders:

```bash
echo $PATH
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
```
screens.question: `which python3` prints the full path of the program `python3` would run. What does Ana see?

options.why: You picked the Mac's own Python. `which` reports the winner of the search, the copy in folder 1.
You expected a list of every copy. Plain `which` names only the one that would run.

hints.text: `which` runs the same search as the shell, then reports the result.
The search ends here.
Folder 1 is `/usr/local/bin`, so the answer is that folder plus `/python3`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. `which` names the program the search finds first.

explain.text: You joined folder 1 and the name: `/usr/local/bin/python3`. When two copies exist, `which` settles which one you are really running. It is the first thing to type when a command misbehaves.

screens.prose: VS Code comes with a command, `code`, that opens a folder: `code .` opens the current one. Ana types it and gets `zsh: command not found: code`. VS Code is installed.

state.caption: Not on the PATH: the folder holding code

screens.question: Why can the shell not find `code`?

options.text: The folder holding `code` is not on her PATH
VS Code did not install properly
options.why: You read "not found" as "not installed". The program is on her disk; the shell just never opens its folder.
You treated `code` as a script. It is a program, and the shell found no program of that name in folders 1 to 3.

hints.text: Which folders does the shell open?
`code` sits in a folder outside the chain of arrows.
The shell searched folders 1, 2 and 3, found no `code`, and gave up.

feedback.correct: The search covers only the PATH, and VS Code's folder is not on it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether the folder holding `code` is one the shell searches.

explain.text: You saw `code` sitting outside the chain of arrows. "Command not found" means no folder on the PATH holds that name. On a Mac, VS Code's command palette offers "Install 'code' command in PATH" to fix it.

screens.prose:
Ana wants to try the Mac's own Python once. She types its full path:

```bash
/usr/bin/python3 --version
```
screens.question: What does the terminal print?

options.why: You let the PATH order decide. A command containing `/` is run from exactly that path, with no search.
You expected only bare names to work. A full path always runs, as long as the file is there.

hints.text: Does the shell need to search when you give it the exact folder?
The path points straight at this program.
A command with a `/` in it skips the PATH, so `/usr/bin/python3` runs the 3.9 copy.

feedback.correct: A full path skips the search and runs that exact file.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether a search is needed at all.

explain.text: You noticed the slash. A command containing `/` names its file directly, so the shell skips the PATH. That is how to reach a copy the search would hide.

screens.prose: On a new laptop with no Python, Ana opens window A at 9:00. At 9:10 she installs Python, and the installer adds its folder to her PATH settings. At 9:20 she opens window B.
screens.question: What should Ana do about window A?

options.text: Close it and use a new window

options.why: You took the error as a failed install. Window B proves Python is installed; window A read its PATH before the install.
A restart works, but only because it closes window A. Opening a new window is enough.

options.text: Add Python's folder to the PATH settings again
options.why: You added it twice. The settings already have it; window A read them before they changed.

hints.text: Why does window B work when window A does not?
Compare the times. Which window opened after the install?
A window reads the PATH once, when it opens. Window A read it at 9:00, before Python's folder was added.

feedback.correct: A new window reads the new PATH.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about when each window read its PATH.

byKey.reinstall: You blamed the install, as most people do. Window B runs Python fine. Window A simply read its PATH at 9:00, before the change.

explain.text: You compared the opening times. Each window copies the PATH when it opens and keeps that copy. Window A's copy is from before the install, so it can never find Python.

screens.prose: Every time, the shell did the same thing. It opened the PATH folders left to right and ran the first program with the name typed: $$\text{runs} = \text{first folder on the PATH that holds the name}$$ No such folder means `command not found`.
screens.question: Ana's PATH is `/home/ana/bin:/usr/bin`, and both folders hold a program called `report`. Which one runs?

options.why: You picked the system folder. The search starts at the left of the PATH, at `/home/ana/bin`.

options.text: Neither: two matches is an error
options.why: You expected the shell to object. It never sees the second copy, because it stops at the first.

hints.text: Which folder comes first in the PATH?
The search starts at the left: `/home/ana/bin` holds `report`, so that one runs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the PATH from the left.

explain.text: You read the PATH from the left and stopped at the first folder holding `report`. Putting a folder at the front of the PATH lets its programs win. Putting it at the back lets others win.

screens.prose: Write the shell's search as steps, as it would carry them out.
screens.question: Put the steps in order, first at the top.

lines.text: Read the command name you typed
If the name contains `/`, run that exact file and stop
Open the first folder on the PATH
If it holds a program with that name, run it and stop
Otherwise open the next folder and repeat the step above
If no folders are left, print `command not found`

hints.text: Which check lets the shell skip the search entirely?
The slash check comes before any folder is opened.
Read, slash check, first folder, match check, next folder, give up.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step uses what the step before it found.

byKey.d3: You opened a folder before checking for a slash. A name with `/` never needs the search, so that check comes first.
byKey.d6: You gave up too early. The shell only says `command not found` after every folder has been checked.

explain.text: Read the name, check for a slash, then walk the PATH folder by folder. Stopping at the first match is why order matters. Giving up only at the end is what `command not found` means.

screens.prose: Ana schedules her backtest to run each night at 22:00 with `python3 backtest.py`. Scheduled jobs start with a short PATH: `/usr/bin:/bin`. The backtest needs Python 3.10 or newer.

state.caption: Arrows: the order in Ana's own terminal

screens.question: Tap the `python3` that the nightly job runs.

hints.text: Which folders are on the job's PATH, and in what order?
The job's PATH starts here: `/usr/local/bin` is not on it.
Searching `/usr/bin` first finds the Mac's Python 3.9, which is too old for the backtest.

feedback.correct: The job finds Python 3.9 in `/usr/bin`, which is too old.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Search only the folders on the job's PATH.

byKey.lb-py: You used Ana's own PATH. The job's PATH has no `/usr/local/bin`, so it never sees Python 3.12.

explain.text: You searched only `/usr/bin` and `/bin`, and found Python 3.9 first. The job fails at 22:00 although it works in Ana's terminal. Writing the full path, `/usr/local/bin/python3 backtest.py`, makes the job run the right Python.

ideas: The PATH is an ordered list of folders; the shell opens them left to right and runs the first program with the name you typed.
`command not found` means no PATH folder holds that name. The program may still be on the disk.
A window reads the PATH when it opens, and a command with a `/` skips the search altogether.

formula.name: Which program runs
formula.tex: \text{runs} = \text{first folder on the PATH that holds the name}
formula.note: `which name` shows the winner; `echo $PATH` shows the list.

summary.trap: A window opened before an install still has the old PATH: open a new window, do not reinstall.

quiz.prose: Ana's PATH is `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin`. A program called `jq` sits in `/usr/bin` and in `/bin`.
quiz.question: Which `jq` runs when she types `jq`?

options.why: You picked the last copy. The shell stops at the first folder that holds `jq`.
You stopped after one folder. The shell moves on to `/usr/bin` and finds it there.

feedback.correct: Folder 1 has none, folder 2 has one: that runs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Walk the PATH from the left.

explain.text: `/usr/local/bin` holds no `jq`, so the shell moves on. `/usr/bin` holds one, and the search stops there.

quiz.prose: The terminal prints `zsh: command not found: pytest`.
quiz.question: What does that tell you for certain?

options.text: No folder on the PATH holds a program called `pytest`

options.why: You read "not found" as "not installed". It may be on the disk, in a folder the PATH leaves out.
You blamed the terminal. It searched as usual and found nothing by that name.

feedback.correct: The search failed; that is all it says.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about where the shell searched.

explain.text: The shell searched every PATH folder and found no `pytest`. It might be installed elsewhere, or not at all. `which` and a look at the PATH tell you which.

quiz.prose: Ana installs a tool, and the installer adds its folder to her PATH settings. In the terminal window she already had open, the tool is not found.
quiz.question: What is the simplest fix?

options.why: You blamed the install. The old window just read its PATH before the change.
Speed does not matter. The old window's PATH does not include the new folder.

feedback.correct: A new window reads the updated PATH.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about when the old window read its PATH.

explain.text: A window reads the PATH once, when it opens. The old window's copy predates the install. A new window picks up the new folder.

quiz.prose: Ana's PATH is `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin`. Each folder holds its own `python3`.
quiz.question: How can she run the copy in `/usr/bin` without changing the PATH?

options.why: Typing it again runs the same search, which stops at `/usr/local/bin` again.
You expected the current folder to count. The shell searches the PATH, not the folder you are in.

feedback.correct: A path with a slash skips the search.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a way to skip the search.

explain.text: A command containing `/` is run from exactly that path. The PATH is not searched at all. The current folder does not change which `python3` the search finds.
